claim: A chain of transfer tests, each built to remove one named rival explanation while keeping the task logic fixed, is stronger evidence than a single pass (Taylor 2009: 3 of 6 crows solved the tube, then passed cue-removal transfers and a new-looking table).
agent_test: For each task class, build an ordered ladder of held-out variants (strip a cue, rename, change surface form, keep logic). Compare plain model vs scaffold at equal tokens on pass-through-ladder rate, not on the first rung.

claim: The decisive control was a transfer with a different surface (trap-table vs trap-tube): all 3 solvers chose correctly on trial 1, all 3 tube-failures and 8 naive crows failed it, which argues against prior hole-avoidance. Based on N=3 solvers in one lab.
agent_test: Run the held-out check in a different surface form than the fitting examples (different notation, domain words, grid vs text) and require first-attempt success; count how often fitted answers die there.

claim: Passing one trap-type task is weak evidence of causal understanding: success does not predict success on a sister task (apes r=0.13, n=20), rooks fail far transfers (6 of 7), and crows fail the non-functional trap transfer (3 of 3).
agent_test: Never accept a pass on one phrasing. Require a pass on at least two structurally matched but visually different variants before S8 accepts; measure the false-accept rate against single-variant acceptance.
audit_note: Rooks 6 of 7 failing far transfers is correct (Seed et al. 2006, PubMed 16581516) but that paper is not among the listed evidence lines; ape r=0.13 n=20 and 3 of 3 crows failing the functional/non-functional trap transfer verified.

claim: A failed control narrows the surviving explanation rather than only refuting understanding: crows did not avoid the trap when a bare hole and a functional trap were compared (consistent with using the hole as the cue), and in the no-water platform control 95% of objects crows dropped were solid, which suggests the Aesop solidity result may reflect an object preference rather than understanding of water displacement (a hypothesis needing further testing).
agent_test: When a held-out check fails, have code record which feature was the cue (ablate one feature at a time) and write it as the lesson line, instead of a generic 'failed'.
audit_note: Taylor 2009 (crows did not avoid trap with hole plus functional trap) and Logan 2014 (95% of objects dropped solid in no-water platform) verified, but Logan et al. only suggest a possible object bias needing further testing, so 'reduces to an object preference' is too strong; Taylor 'used the hole as the cue' is the authors' interpretation.
claim_before_audit: A failed control narrows the surviving explanation rather than only refuting understanding: crows failed when the trap base was removed (they used the hole as the cue), and in the platform control crows chose solid over hollow 95% with no water, so the Aesop 'solidity understanding' reduces to an object preference.

claim: A pre-existing bias that points at the correct answer inflates apparent understanding. When it was set against the correct answer, crows passed 0 of 5 (children 80% in trials 1-5); LLMs show the same: GPT-4 cipher decoding 51% for likely outputs vs 13% for unlikely ones.
agent_test: Build counter-prior items (the correct answer is the unlikely one, or the default heuristic fails). Report accuracy separately on prior-aligned vs prior-opposed items; the gap measures how much the scaffold relies on the prior.
audit_note: Crows 0/5 (Miller 2016) and GPT-4 cipher 51% vs 13% (McCoy) verified; carrying the crow finding over to LLMs is an analogy (output-probability effect), not the same mechanism.

claim: Tasks that pair an arbitrary link with a causal link (same discrimination, different reward logic) test associative learning directly, but results are mixed: stone size 88% large vs 46% in a matched search task, yet water vs sand 58% vs 56% at group level in one study and 76.3% in another.
agent_test: Pair each rule-based task with an arbitrary-mapping twin of equal surface complexity; if scaffold gains also appear on the twin, the gain is not rule use.

claim: The hidden-causal-agent result in crows (8 birds, inspection UCA > HCA, p=0.002) did not replicate with 14 crows and counterbalanced orders (replication n=4, 8.69 vs 10.95 inspections/min, p=.12; pooled p=.15). Commentaries had flagged order and sensitisation confounds in advance.
agent_test: Pre-register an order-counterbalanced replication of any scaffold gain on a fresh problem sample before keeping the element (G7); treat a gain that needs a fixed order as unconfirmed.

claim: The classic string-pulling 'insight' result depends partly on a perceptual-motor feedback loop: when visual feedback is removed (crows, pull-step ratio 96.5% to 55.7%) or the food does not move on the correct pull (crows fail a horizontal two-string task; kea at chance, 7/20 to 12/20), success drops. A redesign with hidden stages let 4 of 11 crows pass, so the loop is not the whole story. Independent labs (Moscow 2025: 6 hooded crows, loose string; Cambridge 2022: 4 jays, mirror string) report slow learning and cannot separate understanding from feedback; no independent lab was found that settles it.
agent_test: For tool or code tasks, hide intermediate feedback (no partial output shown) in the held-out check and see whether the scaffold's gain survives.

claim: Tiny samples limit what animal controls can show: a Wilcoxon test with n=4 cannot go below p=0.0625; key transfers rest on 3 birds; replication groups had 3 to 4 birds; the 10 of 12 first-trial count is 3 birds x 4 transfers, not independent.
agent_test: Size our own control sets so the smallest possible p is below the decision threshold; use at least 30 held-out items per class and report intervals, not only pass/fail.

claim: Counterfactual-world tasks (same procedure, changed rule, e.g. base-9 addition, 1-based indexing, swapped pieces) lower the accuracy of GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude and PaLM-2 below default, while comprehension checks show the models grasp the new rules; default and counterfactual scores correlate, pointing to memorised procedures.
agent_test: Make a counterfactual twin for each benchmark class (change a constant or rule), run scaffold and plain model at equal tokens and compare the default-minus-counterfactual gap. A scaffold that shrinks the gap is doing more than recall.

claim: Letter-string analogies reported solved by GPT-3 collapse with permuted or symbol alphabets (humans stay high), and a synthetic alphabet drops GPT-3 below 0.1 on four of six problem types; two independent groups report this.
agent_test: Test the analogy operator (O7) with re-coded symbols; accept a mapping only if code confirms it on a recoded copy.
audit_note: Verified; note Webb et al. 2024 reply argues the permuted-alphabet gap is a counting-cost issue and GPT-4 with code reaches human level, a caveat the claim omits.

claim: Small logic-preserving edits to theory-of-mind vignettes break model answers: GPT-3.5 still said chocolate with P=95% when the bag was transparent; GPT-4 scored 97% on original false-belief items but fell to 0% on transparent-access and 'inon' categories. Ullman's first report of a flip on one prompt was a double-space artefact and was corrected.
agent_test: Before trusting a pass on an inference item, run code-generated surface perturbations (names, container, order) that keep the answer or flip it deterministically; test prompt-format noise (whitespace) first.
audit_note: Ullman (ar5iv v-latest: 95% chocolate on transparent bag; correction note about double space before 'Sam finds the bag' present) and Shapira (GPT-4 97.5% original; 0% on transparent access and in-to-on in unexpected-transfer task) verified; note the 0% figures are for the unexpected-transfer task.

claim: Whether newer models pass logic-preserving ToM perturbations is not settled: Kosinski built matched true-belief controls into 40 tasks and reports GPT-4 at 75%, while perturbation studies report failures on older models. The control sets differ, so they do not directly conflict. 2026 follow-ups (d10, d11) still test only open models up to Llama-3-70B and DBRX, none reached full robustness, and reasoning fine-tuning amplified a wording shortcut; no 2025 reasoning-model run of Ullman or Shapira sets was found.
agent_test: Re-run the Ullman and Shapira perturbation sets on the current model before relying on any ToM-style gain.

claim: Adding an irrelevant but plausible clause (GSM-NoOp) lowers accuracy in all tested models, by 17.5 points (o1-preview) up to about 65 points (weakest); changing only numbers lowers accuracy and widens the spread across instantiations, though GPT-4o is nearly unchanged under number swaps (95.0 vs 94.9). Newer evidence: an audit of distractors (blog, unreviewed) finds that when only truly irrelevant clauses are kept, drops for GPT-4o, Opus 4.6 and Haiku 4.5 are 0 to 2 points; R1 error rises only from 1.5% to 4.5% with adversarial triggers; distractor count gives a dose-response (K31).
agent_test: Add a distractor-clause variant of each held-out item (code inserts a related but unused quantity) and measure the drop with and without S1 restate-and-strip.

claim: A freshly written matched benchmark (GSM1k; 1,205 items per c25, 1,000 per b25, see critique) shows contamination in some families: drops up to 8%, r2=0.36 between the likelihood of generating GSM8k items and the gap; frontier families show little overfit. Item count confirmed from the paper body: 1,205 problems. Human distinguishability 21.83% (chance 20%). The Razeghi frequency effect needs pretraining counts and was not found tested on frontier models.
agent_test: Hold back a never-published problem set of our own for G7 comparisons and check model familiarity (can it complete a benchmark item verbatim).
audit_note: Minor: the r2=0.36 is labelled Spearman r^2 in the abstract but the body gives Spearman 0.36 and Pearson r2 0.26; 1,205 items, 21.83% vs 20%, up to 8% drop and frontier-model finding verified; Razeghi untested-on-frontier is a negative search result, not verifiable.

claim: Output probability, input probability and the pretraining frequency of numbers change accuracy on deterministic tasks (rot-13 vs other shifts, GPT-3.5 0.21 vs 0.00; GPT-J gap above 70 points between frequent and rare terms).
agent_test: Stratify held-out items by familiarity (round vs odd numbers, common vs rare strings); a scaffold that helps only on familiar strata has not changed reasoning.

claim: Stated reasoning is not a reliable window onto the cause of an answer: a biasing feature (answer always A, suggested answer) changed predictions by up to 36% across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks while the chain of thought never mentioned it. Newer evidence: reasoning models verbalise a used hint 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) to 39% (R1) of the time; but a no-hint paired-question test finds R1 0.37% and Sonnet 3.7 thinking 0.04% unfaithful pairs, and a critique says hint verbalisation confuses incompleteness with unfaithfulness when token budgets are tight.
agent_test: Test whether selection decisions that cite reasons survive a biasing-feature insertion; keep decisions in code (G5).

claim: Reported intrinsic self-correction gains came from oracle labels: with the oracle, GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 95.5; without it, accuracy stays flat or drops (CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1).
agent_test: In S5 tests, run revisions with and without code-supplied failing output at equal tokens; confirm gains vanish without the real signal.

claim: Models show human-like content effects on logic tasks (better when meaning supports the logic), so content is an alternative explanation to logical competence; abstract versions are the control.
agent_test: For each logic item, make an abstract-symbol twin and a belief-incongruent twin; compare.

claim: Single-question benchmarks overstate ability: on FANToM (six question types about the same information) models score well on individual question types but far below humans when all must be answered consistently; on BigToM (procedurally generated ToM items with 25 controls) GPT-4 follows human inference patterns but less reliably than humans, and other models struggle.
agent_test: Ask 3 to 6 differently phrased questions that all depend on the same inference; accept only if code finds them consistent.
audit_note: FANToM (six question types; far below humans when all types must be right) verified, but BigToM (25 controls, 5,000 items) reports GPT-4 aligned closely with human inference patterns and only less reliable, with weaker models struggling, so 'large gaps to humans' does not hold for both benchmarks.
claim_before_audit: Single-question benchmarks overstate ability; consistency across several question types about the same situation (FANToM six types; procedurally generated ToM items with 25 controls) shows large gaps to humans.

claim: Comprehension and trivial-item checks separate 'cannot do the task' from 'did not understand the task': ConceptARC minimal tasks (humans 0.95; GPT-4 text 0.69), permuted-alphabet comprehension checks, and exclusion of 12 of 482 human subjects who failed attention checks.
agent_test: Include trivial control items in each held-out set; if the scaffold fails them, set aside its failure on harder items as a comprehension problem.
audit_note: The 12 of 482 exclusion was reported by Moskvichev et al. and quoted by Mitchell et al.; humans 0.95 and GPT-4 text 0.69 verified.

claim: Shortcuts hide in the data: a horse classifier relied on a source tag in about one fifth of horse images; Winograd-style tests lost validity after public release; baselines that remove the question or the candidates reveal the shortcut.
agent_test: Before scoring a class, run baselines with the question removed or the key field masked; if they score above chance the item set has a shortcut.

claim: Best-practice rule: list the known shortcuts before running a study, add a control that omits the question, and prefer many varied tasks to one famous item.
agent_test: Write the shortcut list for each problem class into the S0 gate table and attach one control per shortcut.
audit_note: Ivanova rules 2/3/4/13 support all three practices; Heyes is only loosely related.

claim: A single failed control can mean the task demands were too heavy, not that the ability is missing: with fewer objects (4 instead of 12), 4 of 6 crows chose the narrow tube and 3 switched when the water was higher. This conflicts with Ullman's rule that one principled failure outweighs many successes.
agent_test: When a variant fails, run a simplified rescue version (fewer distractors, shorter input). If it passes, record the failure as load-related, not as missing rule use.

claim: Apes' false-belief anticipatory looks were tested against a low-level cueing account with an inanimate control: 22 of 43 looked at a box vs 22 of 30 in the original; first looks to target 14 of 22 (p=0.28). Heyes argues for associative or submentalizing accounts by default; neither side's default is justified. Re-opened (d01): numbers confirmed (43 apes, 22 looked, 14 of 22 first looks to target, p=0.28; original 22 of 30). Low power: more than half the apes made no look. The inanimate control is the design the authors offer; the Heyes side was not read (d02), so the dispute is not shown to be settled.
agent_test: Match each social-reasoning test with a cue-only control (same visual or textual cue, no agent) and compare.

claim: Hidden test sets that agents cannot train on are a standard from animal testing: the Animal-AI testbed uses controlled tasks and withheld tests.
agent_test: Keep the held-out set unseen by any prompt-tuning loop; log every time it is consulted.

claim: First-trial success alone is not diagnostic: Tiga failed trial 1 of transfer 2 then avoided the trap in the next 19 trials, and succeeded on trial 1 of transfer 3 but then performed at chance.
agent_test: Use blocks of at least 10 held-out items rather than the first attempt alone, but also record the first attempt, since fitting without understanding shows up later.

claim: A tool step can remove a default-versus-counterfactual gap: GPT-4 with code execution solved permuted-alphabet letter-string analogies at human level (P=0.496 vs humans, N=99 and 97 humans), where plain GPT-4 was worse (P=8.9e-13). The authors read the gap as a counting load, not missing analogy. Not tested at equal tokens.
agent_test: For each counterfactual item class, run plain, code-assisted and reflection arms with a token cap; count a scaffold as helping only if the gap (default minus counterfactual) shrinks, not if both rise.

claim: A model can pass most single variants and still fail almost every problem across variants. GSM-IC (code-davinci-002): micro accuracy 72.4% vs macro (all variants right) 6.0% for plain CoT. ToM scenarios (four open models): per-question accuracy 58 to 74% vs all-scenes-right 0 to 4.4%.
agent_test: Score the held-out check as all-variants-pass per problem. Compare the single-variant false-pass rate with the all-variants rate on our own tasks to find how many variants are enough; no external false-accept curve exists.
audit_note: Minor: ToM figure is turn accuracy vs goal accuracy (all scenes of a scenario right) on 68 scenarios.

claim: Cheap input hygiene helps some, sampling helps more. GSM-IC (code-davinci-002): adding the sentence "Feel free to ignore irrelevant information" lifted CoT micro accuracy 72.4 to 77.8 and macro 6.0 to 15.0; 20-sample self-consistency reached 88.1 and 30.0 (20x tokens). A restate-and-strip step was not tested.
agent_test: Add three arms to the distractor held-out set: baseline, ignore-sentence, restate-and-strip; log tokens. Prior: expect a few points, not a fix.

claim: Failure on perturbed items scales with the amount of distraction, so a failed control can reflect load. GSM-DC at reasoning depth 5: Grok-3-Beta step accuracy 43% with one irrelevant node to 19% with fifteen; GPT-4.1 26% to 2%. Same direction as the crow rescue version (K24); the LLM rescue test (cut distractors, rerun the same item) was not run in these papers.
agent_test: When a perturbed item fails, rerun it with distractors or length cut by half. If it passes, log "load-related failure", not "rule missing"; if it still fails, treat it as a real failure.
audit_note: Yang et al. 2025 numbers verified; the no-rescue-test caveat is correct (paper has no same-item ablation).

claim: Distractor controls need their own audit: only 117 of 945 (12.4%) model-written NoOp clauses were judged truly irrelevant by one auditor (kappa 0.32 between two auditors), and on that audited set drops for three current models were 0 to 2 points. Adversarial irrelevant triggers still raise R1 error from 1.5% to 4.5% and lengthen answers (o1 26.4% of cases >1.5x budget).
agent_test: Have a second model or a person check that each distractor cannot change the answer before it enters the held-out set; log the share rejected.

claim: For G10 on current long-reasoning models, hint insertion alone is weak and paired-input consistency is the cleaner test. Hint verbalisation: 25% (Claude 3.7) and 39% (R1); no-hint swapped-question test: R1 0.37%, Sonnet 3.7 thinking 0.04% of 4,834 pairs; a critique shows verbalisation rises up to 90% with larger budgets in small open models.
agent_test: Run a swapped-question consistency check on our decision steps with a generous token budget; use hint insertion only with k samples and a causal check.

claim: Accuracy alone overstates rule use on ARC-style tasks. ConceptARC text, o3 77.1% (medium effort): about 27% of correct outputs rest on correct-unintended or incorrect rules (Claude about 19%, humans about 7%); in images o3 had 29.2% output accuracy but 40.0% correct-intended rules. No head-to-head test of colour permutation, input mutation and symmetry checks exists.
agent_test: On our ARC-style set, have the agent state its rule, then compare false-pass rate under each control (colour permutation, input mutation, symmetry flip) against a rule audit; choose by false passes removed per token.

claim: Contamination can be checked cheaply, but not by the Razeghi method on frontier models. Usable: a fresh matched set (GSM1k, 1,205 items; humans picked the new item 21.83% vs 20% chance), likelihood of old items (r2=0.36 with the gap), and a per-model perturbation gap (Haiku 4.5 on GSM-Symbolic: 1.3 point drop). Razeghi needs pretraining term counts and was not found tested on frontier models.
agent_test: Write 30 fresh items matched to each benchmark class, run the distinguishability audit, and compare pass rates old vs fresh with a bootstrap over problem templates.
audit_note: Minor: 'cheaply' is the author's gloss (GSM1k needed a fresh annotated set); 1,205 items, 21.83% vs 20%, r2 0.36 (same Spearman caveat as K15) and Haiku 4.5 CoT 1.3 point drop (PAL 1.7, SBSC 1.4) verified; Razeghi method needs pretraining term counts.

claim: A perturbed set must be matched to the original on difficulty cues. In GSM-Symbolic the new variants hold larger numbers (K-S 0.12, p<0.001); only 8 of 20 open-weight models show a significant drop, and controlling for number size removes half of the rest.
agent_test: Before reading a perturbation drop, compare number magnitude, token length and step count of original and perturbed items; bootstrap over problem templates.

claim: Name and number swaps no longer separate scaffolds on a current model: Claude Haiku 4.5 on 1,000 GSM-Symbolic pairs lost 1.3 points with CoT, 1.7 with single-shot code and 1.4 with iterative code (p=.096). Code scaffolds did not shrink the gap, because it was already near zero.
agent_test: Use changed-rule counterfactuals and distractors, not name/number swaps, as the held-out variants on current models.

claim: Paired-answer controls catch order effects: GPT-4 on story analogies was 89% (16 of 18) when the correct story was listed first and 61% (11 of 18) when second. A counterfactual comprehension check (ask the new alphabet order in isolation) showed GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 understood the setup, so their failure was not misunderstanding.
agent_test: For every forced-choice held-out item, run both answer orders and add a setup-comprehension probe; count only order-stable answers.
